title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 1: GPT Pretraining
text:
This is the first post in a three-part series on building a large language model from scratch. Training a modern, instruction-following LLM happens in three stages:

Pretraining: Teaching the model to predict the next token over a large corpus of raw text.
Instruction tuning: Fine-tuning the pretrained model on instruction/response pairs so that it learns to follow instructions.
Preference tuning: Aligning the model with human preferences via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 1: GPT Pretraining
text:
Multihead Attention
The purpose of self-attention is to allow the model to attend to different parts of the input sequence, learning which tokens are most relevant for computing the representation of any given token. Mathematically, it is implemented as a scaled dot-product between Query and Key vectors. We scale the dot product by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) to keep its magnitude from growing too large, which would otherwise push the softmax into regions with vanishingly small gradients and hinder training.
Formally, self-attention is defined as:
\[
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}})V
\]
Where:

\(Q\) (Query): A matrix representing the element we are currently looking “at.”
\(K\) (Key): A matrix representing all elements the Query is compared against.
\(V\) (Value): A matrix containing the information associated with each Key.
\(d_k\): The dimension of the key vectors.

As in BERT, attention is applied multiple times in parallel through Multi-Head Attention, with each head operating in a different subspace so the model can attend to different types of relationships simultaneously. The outputs from all heads are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension.
The critical difference from the encoder is the mask. Because GPT generates text autoregressively, a token must never attend to tokens that come after it, otherwise the model could trivially “cheat” by peeking at the very answer it is supposed to predict. We enforce this with a causal mask: an upper-triangular matrix that sets the attention scores for all future positions to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, driving their attention weights to zero. As with BERT, we apply dropout to the attention weights before the output projection.

class MultiHeadAttention(nnx.Module):
    """Multi-head self-attention module"""
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads, dropout_rate, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        assert d_model % num_heads == 0, f"d_model ({d_model}) must be divisible by num_heads ({num_heads})"
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.head_dim = d_model // num_heads
        self.q_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.k_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.v_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.out_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)

        self.dropout = nnx.Dropout(rate=dropout_rate, rngs=rngs)

    def _split_heads(self, x, batch, seq_len):
        return x.reshape(batch, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)

    def __call__(self, x):
        batch, seq_len, _ = x.shape
        mask = jnp.triu(jnp.ones((seq_len, seq_len), dtype=bool), 1)

        q = self._split_heads(self.q_proj(x), batch, seq_len)
        k = self._split_heads(self.k_proj(x), batch, seq_len)
        v = self._split_heads(self.v_proj(x), batch, seq_len)

        attn_logits = jnp.matmul(q, k.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2)) / jnp.sqrt(self.head_dim)
        attn_logits = jnp.where(mask, -jnp.inf, attn_logits)

        attn_weights = jax.nn.softmax(attn_logits, axis=-1)
        attn_weights = self.dropout(attn_weights)
        out = jnp.matmul(attn_weights, v).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(batch, seq_len, self.d_model)
        return self.out_proj(out)

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 1: GPT Pretraining
Building a Large Language ModelPart 1: GPT Pretraining
text:
Transformer Block
We now assemble these components into a single, reusable Transformer block. We use the Pre-LayerNorm architecture: layer normalization is applied before each sublayer rather than after. The input is normalized, passed through multi-head attention, regularized with dropout, and then added back to the original input through a residual connection. The same pattern repeats for the feed-forward network.
Layer normalization stabilizes training by ensuring each sublayer receives inputs with a consistent distribution, mitigating vanishing and exploding gradients, while the residual connections provide a clean gradient path through the depth of the network.

class TransformerBlock(nnx.Module):
    """Single Transformer block consisting of multi-head self-attention followed by a feedforward network, with residual connections and layer normalization."""
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads, d_ff, mha_dropout_rate, dropout_rate, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, num_heads, mha_dropout_rate, rngs=rngs)
        self.norm1 = nnx.LayerNorm(d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.ffn = FeedForward(d_model, d_ff, rngs=rngs)
        self.norm2 = nnx.LayerNorm(d_model, rngs=rngs)

        self.dropout = nnx.Dropout(rate=dropout_rate, rngs=rngs)

    def __call__(self, x):
        shortcut = x
        x = self.norm1(x)
        x = self.attention(x)
        x = self.dropout(x)
        x = x + shortcut

        shortcut = x
        x = self.norm2(x)
        x = self.ffn(x)
        x = self.dropout(x)
        x = x + shortcut
        return x







Note



The original GPT used a Post-LayerNorm arrangement, but GPT-2 and most modern decoder-only models moved to Pre-LayerNorm, which has been shown to improve training stability in deep Transformers.

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 1: GPT Pretraining
text:
GPT Model
With the Transformer block in hand, we can assemble the full GPT model. We begin with token and learned positional embeddings: the token embedding maps each token ID to a vector, while the positional embedding gives the model a sense of where each token sits in the sequence. The two are summed and passed through dropout before entering the stack of Transformer blocks. After the final block, we apply one last layer normalization and project the result to the vocabulary size with a linear output head, producing a logit for every possible next token at each position.

class GPT(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, config: GPTConfig, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        # Token and Position Embeddings
        self.token_emb = nnx.Embed(config["vocab_size"], config["d_model"], rngs=rngs)
        self.pos_emb = nnx.Param(jax.random.normal(rngs.params(), (1, config["context_length"], config["d_model"])) * 0.02)
        self.drop_emb = nnx.Dropout(rate=config["dropout_rate"], rngs=rngs)

        # Transformer Blocks
        self.blocks = nnx.List([TransformerBlock(config["d_model"], config["num_heads"], config["d_ff"], config["mha_dropout_rate"], config["dropout_rate"], rngs=rngs) for _ in range(config["num_layers"])])
        self.norm_final = nnx.LayerNorm(config["d_model"], rngs=rngs)

        # Logits
        self.out_head = nnx.Linear(config["d_model"], config["vocab_size"], rngs=rngs)

    def __call__(self, input_ids):
        _, seq_len = input_ids.shape

        # Combine embeddings: Token + Position
        x = self.token_emb(input_ids)
        x = x + self.pos_emb[:, :seq_len, :]

        x = self.drop_emb(x)
        for block in self.blocks:
            x = block(x)
        x = self.norm_final(x)
        logits = self.out_head(x)
        return logits

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 1: GPT Pretraining
Building a Large Language ModelPart 1: GPT Pretraining
text:
Greedy Decoding
With a trained model in hand, we can finally generate text. Our model takes a sequence of token IDs and outputs logits over the vocabulary for each position, so to turn it into a text generator we need two things: a way to move between text and token IDs, and a decoding strategy that chooses the next token from the logits.
We start with two small helpers. text_to_token_ids encodes a string into token IDs and adds a leading batch dimension with [None, :], since the model expects batched input. token_ids_to_text reverses this, squeezing out the batch dimension before decoding back to a string.
The decoding strategy itself lives in generate_text_simple. This is greedy decoding: at every step we pick the single most probable next token. We generate one token at a time for max_new_tokens steps. On each iteration we crop the running sequence to the last context_size tokens with idx_cond so we never exceed the model’s context window, then pass it through the model to obtain logits. We only care about the prediction for the final position, so we slice out logits[:, -1, :], and jnp.argmax selects the highest-scoring token in the vocabulary. We append that token to the sequence with jnp.concatenate and feed the extended sequence back in on the next step. Because we always take the argmax, this procedure is deterministic: the same prompt will always produce the same continuation.

def text_to_token_ids(text: str, tokenizer) -> np.ndarray:
    return np.array(tokenizer.encode(text, allowed_special={"<|endoftext|>"}))[None, :]

def token_ids_to_text(token_ids: np.ndarray, tokenizer) -> str:
    return tokenizer.decode(token_ids.squeeze())

def generate_text_simple(model, idx, max_new_tokens, context_size):
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        idx_cond = idx[:, -context_size:]
        logits = model(idx_cond)

        logits = logits[:, -1, :]
        idx_next = jnp.argmax(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
        idx = jnp.concatenate((idx, idx_next), axis=1)
    return idx

Before we can generate, we need to reload the weights we saved earlier. We first construct a fresh GPT model with the same configuration, then restore the checkpoint with orbax and write the restored parameters into the model with nnx.update. Finally, we create an evaluation view of the model with deterministic=True so that dropout is disabled during inference.

rngs = nnx.Rngs(0)
model = GPT(config=config, rngs=rngs)

save_directory = Path("./model_checkpoint/GPT_jax")
checkpointer = orbax.PyTreeCheckpointer()
restored_state = checkpointer.restore(
    save_directory.absolute(),
    args=orbax.args.PyTreeRestore(nnx.state(model))
)
nnx.update(model, restored_state)

eval_model = nnx.view(model, deterministic=True)

Now we put it all together. We give the model a prompt, encode it to token IDs, and ask it to generate up to 200 new tokens, decoding the full sequence back to text at the end.
As you can see in the generated text below, while the output is coherent and grammatical, it is very repetitive. This is a common artifact of greedy decoding: because we always pick the single most probable next token, the model can fall into loops. It can be mitigated with sampling-based strategies such as temperature or nucleus (top-p) sampling, or with an explicit repetition penalty. Furthermore, for the prompt “The capital of France is” we might have expected a city name, but the model instead generated a short story about the inhabitants of France. This is because our training corpus was composed of synthetic short stories.

start_context = "The capital of France is"
token_ids = generate_text_simple(
    model=eval_model,
    idx=text_to_token_ids(start_context, tokenizer),
    max_new_tokens=200,
    context_size=config["context_length"]
    )
print("Output text:\n", token_ids_to_text(token_ids, tokenizer))

text: In this post, we explore the architecture of BERT, an encoder-only Transformer model. We will walk through its fundamental components and then implement the model from scratch using JAX and Flax, pretraining it on a subset of the C4 dataset.

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)
text:
Multihead Attention
The purpose of self-attention is to allow the model to attend to different parts of the input sequence. When we say “attend to a part of the input sequence”, we mean that the model learns which tokens are most relevant for computing the representation of other tokens. An example that highlights the importance of self-attention is disambiguating a polysemous word like “bank.” The word “bank” can refer to a financial institution or the side of a river. In order for our model to make accurate predictions about which meaning is intended, it must be able to attend to the surrounding context (e.g., “money” vs. “river”).
Notice how in the examples below how the word bank attends (bigger value) to different words in the sentence depending on whether it refers to a financial institution or the side of a river.

Mathematically, self-attention is implemented as a scaled dot-product. The dot-product serves as a measure of similarity between two vectors (Query and Key). We scale this dot product by dividing it by the square root of the dimensionality of the keys (\(\sqrt{d_k}\)). This scaling is crucial: as the dimensionality increases, the magnitude of the dot products can grow very large, pushing the softmax function into regions with extremely small gradients, which hinders training.
Formally, self-attention can be defined as:
\[
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}})V
\]
Where:

\(Q\) (Query): A matrix representing the current focus or the element we are looking “at.”
\(K\) (Key): A matrix representing all elements in the sequence that the Query is being compared against.
\(V\) (Value): A matrix containing the actual information/content associated with each Key.
\(d_k\): The dimension of the key vectors.

Additionally, self-attention is applied multiple times in parallel through Multi-Head Attention. The input is split into multiple “heads”, each of which performs the attention mechanism in a different subspace. This allows the model to simultaneously attend to different types of relationships (e.g., one head focusing on syntactic dependencies while another focuses on semantic content). The outputs from all heads are concatenated and then passed through a final linear projection to return the tensor to the model’s original dimensionality.
Note that in our implementation, we omit padding tokens from the computation by passing an attention_mask. The mask is used to set the attention scores of padding tokens to \(-\infty\) before the softmax operation. This ensures that the model assigns zero probability to these tokens, preventing them from influencing the representation of actual content. Also note that we apply dropout on the attention weights before projecting the output back to the model dimension.

class MultiHeadAttention(nnx.Module):
    """Multi-head self-attention module as used in the Transformer / BERT encoder.
    Splits the input into multiple attention heads, computes scaled dot-product
    attention for each head, and then projects the concatenated outputs back
    to the model dimension."""
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads, dropout_rate, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.head_dim = d_model // num_heads
        self.q_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.k_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.v_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.out_proj = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)

        self.dropout = nnx.Dropout(rate=dropout_rate, rngs=rngs)

    def __call__(self, x, attention_mask=None):
        batch, seq_len, _ = x.shape

        q = self.q_proj(x).reshape(batch, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
        k = self.k_proj(x).reshape(batch, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
        v = self.v_proj(x).reshape(batch, seq_len, self.num_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)

        attn_logits = jnp.matmul(q, k.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2)) / jnp.sqrt(self.head_dim)
        if attention_mask is not None:
            # BERT Mask: mask 0s are padding, mask 1s are real tokens
            attn_logits = jnp.where(attention_mask == 0, -1e9, attn_logits)

        attn_weights = jax.nn.softmax(attn_logits, axis=-1)
        attn_weights = self.dropout(attn_weights)
        out = jnp.matmul(attn_weights, v).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(batch, seq_len, self.d_model)
        return self.out_proj(out)

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)
text:
Feed Forward Network
The feed forward MLP is quite simple. We have two linear layers with a Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) activation in between.
Notice that the dropout is applied to the output of the first linear layer. This is a common practice in Transformer models.

class FeedForward(nnx.Module):
    """Position-wise feedforward network"""
    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff, dropout_rate, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        self.linear1 = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_ff, rngs=rngs)
        self.linear2 = nnx.Linear(d_ff, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.dropout = nnx.Dropout(rate=dropout_rate, rngs=rngs)

    def __call__(self, x):
        x = self.linear1(x)
        x = jax.nn.gelu(x)
        x = self.dropout(x)
        return self.linear2(x)

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)
text:
Transformer Block
We can now assemble these components into a single, reusable Transformer block. This block follows the architecture described in the original Transformer paper. It begins by applying layer normalization to the input embeddings. Next, we apply multi-head attention, followed by a residual connection that adds the original input back to the attention output. We then apply a second layer of normalization before passing the result through a feedforward network, followed by a final residual connection.
The primary goal of layer normalization is to stabilize the training process. By ensuring that each layer receives inputs with a consistent distribution, we mitigate issues like vanishing or exploding gradients, allowing the model to learn more effectively and converge faster.

class TransformerBlock(nnx.Module):
    """Single Transformer block consisting of multi-head self-attention followed by a feedforward network, with residual connections and layer normalization."""
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_heads, d_ff, mha_dropout_rate, ff_dropout_rate, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, num_heads, mha_dropout_rate, rngs=rngs)
        self.norm1 = nnx.LayerNorm(d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.ffn = FeedForward(d_model, d_ff, ff_dropout_rate, rngs=rngs)
        self.norm2 = nnx.LayerNorm(d_model, rngs=rngs)

    def __call__(self, x, attention_mask=None):
        x = x + self.attention(self.norm1(x), attention_mask=attention_mask)
        x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x))
        return x







Note



We use the Pre-LayerNorm architecture, where normalization is applied before the attention and feed-forward layers, which has been shown to improve training stability in deep transformers. In the original BERT implementation Post-LayerNorm is used instead.

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)
text:
BERT Encoder
Now we are ready to build the encoder. We initialize token and position embeddings and stack a series of Transformer blocks. First, we pass the token IDs through the embedding layer and add the resulting embeddings to the positional embeddings. The output is then passed through a layer normalization step before entering the Transformer blocks. After the final Transformer block, we apply another layer normalization to produce the sequence output. Finally, we extract the first token ([CLS]), pass it through a linear layer with a tanh activation function, and return it as the pooled output, which can be used for classification tasks.

class BERTEncoder(nnx.Module):
    """BERT Encoder consisting of token, and position embeddings followed by a stack of Transformer blocks."""
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, num_heads, num_layers, d_ff, max_seq_len, mha_dropout_rate=0.1, ff_dropout_rate=0.1, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        # Token and Position Embeddings
        self.token_emb = nnx.Embed(vocab_size, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.pos_emb = nnx.Param(jax.random.normal(rngs.params(), (1, max_seq_len, d_model)) * 0.02)

        # Encoder Stack
        self.blocks = nnx.List([TransformerBlock(d_model, num_heads, d_ff, mha_dropout_rate, ff_dropout_rate, rngs=rngs) for _ in range(num_layers)])
        self.norm_final = nnx.LayerNorm(d_model, rngs=rngs)

        # Linear layer used for classification downstream tasks
        self.pooler_dense = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.pooler_act = jax.nn.tanh

        # LayerNorm for input embeddings
        self.embedding_norm = nnx.LayerNorm(d_model, rngs=rngs)

    def __call__(self, input_ids, attention_mask=None):
        # input_ids: (batch, seq_len)
        # mask: (batch, seq_len): 1 for real and 0 for padding

        b, s = input_ids.shape

        # Combine embeddings: Token + Position
        x = self.token_emb(input_ids)
        x = x + self.pos_emb[:, :s, :]
        x = self.embedding_norm(x)

        # Transform the mask for the attention mechanism (this is due to multiple heads)
        # (batch, seq_len) -> (batch, 1, 1, seq_len)
        if attention_mask is not None:
            attn_mask = attention_mask[:, None, None, :]
        else:
            attn_mask = None

        for block in self.blocks:
            x = block(x, attention_mask=attn_mask)

        x = self.norm_final(x)

        # BERT returns the full sequence of hidden states for NER/QA
        # and a "pooled" output for classification
        sequence_output = x

        # Pooled output
        cls_token = x[:, 0, :]
        pooled_output = self.pooler_act(self.pooler_dense(cls_token))

        return sequence_output, pooled_output

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)
text:
Masked Language Modeling
During pre-training, our objective is to predict the masked tokens in our input sequence. To achieve this, we implement an MLM head that processes the normalized sequence output from the BERT encoder.
The MLM head operates by passing the hidden states through a feed-forward network comprising of linear layers and GELU activation, followed by a dropout layer. To produce the final logits, the output is projected back to the vocabulary size using the weights from the input embedding layer. This technique, known as weight tying, reduces the total parameter count and improves regularization by sharing representations between the input and output layers.

class MLMHead(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, vocab_size, embedding_layer, dropout_rate, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        self.linear1 = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.linear2 = nnx.Linear(d_model, d_model, rngs=rngs)
        self.dropout = nnx.Dropout(dropout_rate, rngs=rngs)

        # reference to embedding layer for weight tying
        self.embedding = embedding_layer

        # BERT uses a bias term for vocab projection
        self.bias = nnx.Param(jnp.zeros((vocab_size,)))

    def __call__(self, x):
        x = self.linear1(x)
        x = jax.nn.gelu(x)
        x = self.linear2(x)
        x = self.dropout(x)

        # tied weights
        embed_weights = self.embedding.embedding  # (vocab, d_model)

        logits = jnp.matmul(x, embed_weights.T) + self.bias
        return logits

class BertForMaskedLM(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, num_heads, num_layers, d_ff, max_seq_len, mlm_dropout_rate=0.1, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):

        self.encoder = BERTEncoder(
            vocab_size,
            d_model,
            num_heads,
            num_layers,
            d_ff,
            max_seq_len,
            rngs=rngs
        )

        # pass token embedding for weight tying
        self.mlm_head = MLMHead(
            d_model,
            vocab_size,
            self.encoder.token_emb,
            dropout_rate=mlm_dropout_rate,
            rngs=rngs
        )

    def __call__(self, input_ids, attention_mask=None):
        sequence_output, _ = self.encoder(input_ids, attention_mask)
        logits = self.mlm_head(sequence_output)
        return logits







Note



We add a bias term to the logits as this helps the model learn the baseline frequency of tokens.


To facilitate the MLM task, we apply specific disruptions to the input sequences during training. The algorithm works as follows: first, we select 15% of the tokens in a sequence as candidates for modification. Of these selected tokens, 80% are replaced with a [MASK] token, 10% are replaced with a random token from the vocabulary, and the remaining 10% are left unchanged. We then pass the corrupted text through the model and train it to predict the original tokens based on the surrounding context.
Note that the loss is computed only on the masked tokens, not on the unmasked ones. The figure below depicts these disruptions on the input text (using words rather than token IDs for illustrative purposes).






Figure 2: MLM Algorithm




def apply_mlm_masking(
    rng,
    input_ids,
    attention_mask,
    mask_token_id,
    vocab_ids,
    mask_prob=0.15,
):

    rng_select, rng_replace, rng_random = jax.random.split(rng, 3)

    # candidate token selection of mask_prob
    selection_mask = jax.random.bernoulli(
        rng_select,
        p=mask_prob,
        shape=input_ids.shape
    )

    selection_mask = (
        selection_mask &
        attention_mask.astype(bool)
    )

    mlm_loss_mask = selection_mask.astype(jnp.float32)

    # replacement strategy
    replace_probs = jax.random.uniform(
        rng_replace,
        shape=input_ids.shape
    )

    is_mask = replace_probs < 0.80

    is_random = (
        (replace_probs >= 0.80) &
        (replace_probs < 0.90)
    )

    # random token generation
    random_indices = jax.random.randint(
        rng_random,
        shape=input_ids.shape,
        minval=0,
        maxval=len(vocab_ids),
    )

    random_tokens = vocab_ids[random_indices]

    # apply replacements
    masked_input_ids = input_ids

    # 80% is masked
    masked_input_ids = jnp.where(
        selection_mask & is_mask,
        mask_token_id,
        masked_input_ids
    )

    # 10% is replaced with random tokens
    masked_input_ids = jnp.where(
        selection_mask & is_random,
        random_tokens,
        masked_input_ids
    )

    return masked_input_ids, input_ids, mlm_loss_mask


MLM Loss
The loss function for MLM is a cross-entropy loss between the predicted token probabilities and the ground truth token IDs. However, we only want to compute the loss for the masked tokens. We can achieve this by masking out the loss for non-masked tokens.
Mathematically the loss is defined as: \[\mathcal{L}_{MLM} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \log p(y_i | x)\]
Where:

\(\mathcal{M}\) is the set of indices where tokens were masked.
\(|\mathcal{M}|\) is the total number of masked tokens.
\(y_i\) is the ground truth token ID for position \(i\).
\(p(y_i \mid x)\) is the predicted probability of the correct token.


def mlm_loss_fn(logits, labels, mask):
    """
    logits: (batch, seq_len, vocab_size)
    labels: (batch, seq_len) - the ground truth token IDs
    mask: (batch, seq_len) - 1 for masked tokens, 0 for others
    """
    # Compute the cross-entropy loss for each token
    one_hot_labels = jax.nn.one_hot(labels, logits.shape[-1])
    log_probs = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits, axis=-1)
    loss = -jnp.sum(one_hot_labels * log_probs, axis=-1)

    # Apply the mask so we only penalize predictions on masked tokens
    masked_loss = loss * mask

    # Average loss over the number of masked tokens
    return jnp.sum(masked_loss) / (jnp.sum(mask) + 1e-8)


def compute_loss(model, input_ids, labels, attention_mask, mask):
    logits = model(input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)
    return mlm_loss_fn(logits, labels, mask)

def to_host(x):
    if isinstance(x, jax.Array):
        # Handle PRNG keys specially
        if jax.dtypes.issubdtype(x.dtype, jax.dtypes.prng_key):
            return np.array(jax.random.key_data(x))

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
This is the final post in a three-part series on building a large language model from scratch.
In the previous post we covered the second stage, instruction fine-tuning our pre-trained decoder-only GPT on instruction-response mappings. In this post we tackle the third stage: preference fine-tuning using Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Splitting
With the data in memory, we split it into three sets: 85% for training, 10% for testing, and the remaining 5% for validation. The training set drives the weight updates, the validation set lets us monitor generalization during fine-tuning, and the held-out test set is reserved for the final qualitative evaluation.

train_portion = int(len(data) * 0.85) # 85% for training
test_portion = int(len(data) * 0.1) # 10% for testing
val_portion = len(data) - train_portion - test_portion # 5% for validation
train_data = data[:train_portion]
test_data = data[train_portion:train_portion + test_portion]
val_data = data[train_portion + test_portion:]

print("Training set length:", len(train_data))
print("Validation set length:", len(val_data))
print("Test set length:", len(test_data))

Training set length: 935
Validation set length: 55
Test set length: 110

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Formatting
We reuse the same formatting as we did during instruction fine-tuning.

def format_input(entry):

    instruction_text = (
        f"Below is an instruction that describes a task. "
        f"Write a response that appropriately completes the request."
        f"\n\n### Instruction:\n{entry['instruction']}"
        )

    input_text = (
        f"\n\n### Input:\n{entry['input']}" if entry["input"] else ""
        )
    return instruction_text + input_text

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Loading
Again we load in the same tokenizer as before.

tokenizer = tiktoken.get_encoding("gpt2")

Each dataset entry becomes two token sequences, built exactly like our SFT sequences, one for the chosen response and one for the rejected.
Two details worth mentioning:

We append <|endoftext|> to every sequence. The reward model will read its score at the final token, the only position where causal attention has seen the whole response. This has to hold for every sequence the RM ever sees, so when a pair is too long for allowed_max_length we truncate one token short and put the <|endoftext|> back — otherwise the score would be read at whatever token the cut happened to land on.
We keep a mask of real tokens instead of the -100 label trick we used during instruction fine-tuning. We only need to know where each sequence ends so we can read the score there.

As before we right-pad with <|endoftext|> (id 50256) to the longest sequence in the batch. Right-padding is harmless for a causal model as attention only flows left, so pad positions cannot contaminate real positions. Notice in the collate_fn that we pad the batch to the longest sequence across both the chosen and rejected responses.

PAD_ID = EOS_ID = 50256  # <|endoftext|> plays both roles, as in the previous posts

@dataclass
class PreferenceDataset:
    """Pre-encodes every preference pair; each item holds a chosen and a rejected token sequence."""
    data: list

    def __post_init__(self):
        self.encoded = []
        for entry in self.data:
            prompt = format_input(entry) + "\n\n### Response:\n"
            self.encoded.append({
                "chosen": tokenizer.encode(prompt + entry["chosen"]) + [EOS_ID],
                "rejected": tokenizer.encode(prompt + entry["rejected"]) + [EOS_ID],
            })

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.data)

    def __getitem__(self, idx: int):
        return self.encoded[idx]


def preference_collate_fn(batch, pad_token_id=PAD_ID, allowed_max_length=256):
    longest_seq = max(max(len(item["chosen"]), len(item["rejected"])) for item in batch)
    batch_max_length = min(
        longest_seq,
        allowed_max_length,
    )

    def pad_and_stack(key):
        ids, mask = [], []
        for item in batch:
            seq = item[key]
            if len(seq) > allowed_max_length:
                # A simple truncation would drop the <|endoftext|>
                seq = seq[:allowed_max_length - 1] + [EOS_ID]
            ids.append(np.array(seq + [pad_token_id] * (batch_max_length - len(seq))))
            mask.append(np.array([1.0] * len(seq) + [0.0] * (batch_max_length - len(seq)), dtype=np.float32))
        return np.stack(ids), np.stack(mask)

    chosen_ids, chosen_mask = pad_and_stack("chosen")
    rejected_ids, rejected_mask = pad_and_stack("rejected")
    return chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask

With a dataset and a collate function, we wrap everything in a grain data loader.

def load_and_preprocess_data(data: list, batch_size: int, shuffle=False):

    dataset = PreferenceDataset(data)

    print(f"Loaded {len(dataset)} samples")

    sampler = pygrain.IndexSampler(
        len(dataset),
        shuffle=shuffle,
        seed=42,
        shard_options=pygrain.NoSharding(),
        num_epochs=1,
    )

    dl = pygrain.DataLoader(
        data_source=dataset,
        sampler=sampler,
        operations=[
            pygrain.Batch(batch_size=batch_size, drop_remainder=True, batch_fn=preference_collate_fn)
        ],
    )

    return dl


train_dl = load_and_preprocess_data(data=train_data, batch_size=8, shuffle=True)
val_dl = load_and_preprocess_data(data=val_data, batch_size=8, shuffle=False)

chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask = next(iter(train_dl))
print("chosen_ids:", chosen_ids.shape, " rejected_ids:", rejected_ids.shape)

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Architecture
The architecture of the RM is the same as our instruction-tuned GPT, which already understands the distribution of prompts and responses it will be judging, with one adjustment. We swap the vocabulary head for a scalar head, applied at every position so that it emits one score per token. The position we actually train on is the final <|endoftext|> token, where the model has seen the entire response.

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Loss Function
Our labels are comparisons, not target scores, so we need a model of how latent scores generate observed preferences. The classic answer is the Bradley–Terry model (Bradley and Terry 1952), which states that if the preferred response \(y_w\) has latent quality \(r_w\) and the rejected one \(y_l\) has quality \(r_l\), then
\[P(y_w \succ y_l) = \sigma(r_w - r_l) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(r_w - r_l)}}\]
Maximizing the likelihood of the observed preferences under this model gives our training loss:
\[\mathcal{L}(\phi) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,\, y_w,\, y_l)}\Big[\log \sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big)\Big]\]
Two properties worth noticing:

Only the difference of scores matters. Adding a constant to every score leaves the loss unchanged, so the RM’s absolute scale is arbitrary. This is why, during RL, we will normalize advantages rather than trust raw score magnitudes.
We initialize the scalar head to zeros, so every margin starts at exactly 0 and the initial loss must be exactly \(\ln 2 \approx 0.6931\) (the model is saying “50/50” about every pair).


class RewardModel(nnx.Module):
    """A GPT backbone with a scalar head instead of a vocabulary head.

    Returns one score per position.
    """
    def __init__(self, backbone: GPT, d_model: int, *, rngs: nnx.Rngs):
        self.backbone = backbone
        self.reward_head = nnx.Linear(d_model, 1, kernel_init=nnx.initializers.zeros_init(), rngs=rngs)

    def __call__(self, input_ids):
        h = self.backbone.hidden_states(input_ids)
        return self.reward_head(h).squeeze(-1)  # (batch, seq_len)

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Loading the Instruction-Tuned Model
We restore the GPT-2 medium (Radford et al. 2019) checkpoint saved at the end of the instruction-tuning post.
We will need fresh copies of these weights multiple times in this post, so we wrap the restore in a helper.






Important



Notice that dropout_rate=0.0 which is essential for RLHF



config = GPTConfig(
    vocab_size=tokenizer.n_vocab,
    context_length=256,
    d_model=1024,
    num_heads=16,
    num_layers=24,
    dropout_rate=0.0, # no dropout anywhere in the RLHF stage
    mha_dropout_rate=0.0,
)

SFT_CHECKPOINT = Path("./model_checkpoint/GPT2_jax_sft")

def load_sft_model():
    """A fresh GPT with the instruction-tuned weights restored into it."""
    model = GPT(config=config, rngs=nnx.Rngs(0))
    checkpointer = orbax.PyTreeCheckpointer()
    restored_state = checkpointer.restore(
        SFT_CHECKPOINT.absolute(),
        args=orbax.args.PyTreeRestore(nnx.state(model)),
    )
    nnx.update(model, restored_state)
    return model


reward_model = RewardModel(load_sft_model(), config["d_model"], rngs=nnx.Rngs(1))

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Training the Reward Model
Each step pushes both members of a preference pair through the model, reads the two scores at their final tokens, and applies the Bradley–Terry loss. The margin also gives us a free metric: the fraction of pairs where the chosen response scores higher, the RM’s accuracy, which starts at chance (50%) and should climb well above it.

def reward_at_last_token(rewards, mask):
    """Pick out each sequence's score at its final real token (the <|endoftext|> we appended)."""
    last_idx = jnp.sum(mask, axis=-1).astype(jnp.int32) - 1
    return jnp.take_along_axis(rewards, last_idx[:, None], axis=1).squeeze(-1)


def rm_loss_fn(model, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask):
    r_chosen = reward_at_last_token(model(chosen_ids), chosen_mask)
    r_rejected = reward_at_last_token(model(rejected_ids), rejected_mask)
    margin = r_chosen - r_rejected
    loss = -jnp.mean(jax.nn.log_sigmoid(margin)) # Bradley-Terry negative log-likelihood
    accuracy = jnp.mean((margin > 0).astype(jnp.float32))
    return loss, accuracy


rm_optimizer = nnx.Optimizer(
    reward_model,
    optax.adamw(learning_rate=1e-5, weight_decay=1e-1),
    wrt=nnx.Param,
)


@nnx.jit
def rm_train_step(model, optimizer, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask):
    (loss, accuracy), grads = nnx.value_and_grad(rm_loss_fn, has_aux=True)(
        model, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask
    )
    optimizer.update(model, grads)
    return loss, accuracy


@nnx.jit
def rm_eval_step(model, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask):
    return rm_loss_fn(model, chosen_ids, chosen_mask, rejected_ids, rejected_mask)

One epoch is enough. Reward models overfit quickly, they can start memorizing which surface features separated chosen from rejected in the training set rather than learning the underlying preference, and an overfit RM is dangerous downstream, because PPO will exploit anything it can to maximize the return.

num_epochs = 1
batch_size = 8
num_examples = len(train_data)

eval_freq = 10
eval_iter = 6

rm_loss_history = []
rm_val_loss_history = []
rm_accuracy_history = []
pairs_seen_history = []
pairs_seen = 0
ema_loss = None
val_ema_loss = None
alpha = 0.3

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    train_batch_iter = iter(train_dl)

    for step, batch in tqdm(enumerate(train_batch_iter), total=num_examples // batch_size):
        loss, accuracy = rm_train_step(reward_model, rm_optimizer, *batch)
        pairs_seen += batch[0].shape[0]

        if step > 0 and step % eval_freq == 0:
            loss_val = float(loss)
            ema_loss = loss_val if ema_loss is None else alpha * loss_val + (1 - alpha) * ema_loss
            rm_loss_history.append(ema_loss)
            rm_accuracy_history.append(float(accuracy))
            pairs_seen_history.append(pairs_seen)

            val_losses = [
                float(rm_eval_step(reward_model, *val_batch)[0])
                for val_batch in itertools.islice(iter(val_dl), eval_iter)
            ]
            if val_losses:
                val_ema_loss = (
                    alpha * np.mean(val_losses) + (1 - alpha) * val_ema_loss
                    if val_ema_loss is not None else np.mean(val_losses)
                )
                rm_val_loss_history.append(float(val_ema_loss))




fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
ax.plot(pairs_seen_history, rm_loss_history, color="steelblue", linewidth=1.5, label="train loss")
ax.plot(pairs_seen_history, rm_val_loss_history, color="orange", linewidth=2, label="validation loss")
ax.axhline(np.log(2), color="gray", linewidth=1, linestyle="--", label="chance (ln 2)")
ax.set_xlabel("Preference pairs seen")
ax.set_ylabel("Bradley–Terry loss")

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
section: Language Modeling as a Reinforcement Learning Problem
text:
Language Modeling as a Reinforcement Learning Problem
To apply an RL algorithm we need to phrase generation as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) with the following properties:

State \(s_t\) = the prompt plus the tokens generated so far.
Action \(a_t\) = the next token pulled from a 50,257 (vocabulary size) action space.
Episode = one complete response, ending at <|endoftext|> or a length cap.
Reward: the RM speaks only once, at the end of the episode. The KL constraint is applied per token, giving each action the reward

\[r_t = -\beta \big( \log \pi(a_t \mid s_t) - \log \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a_t \mid s_t) \big) \;+\; \mathbb{1}[t = T] \; r_\phi(x, y)\]
Where the per-token \(\log \pi - \log \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\) is an unbiased single-sample estimate of the KL divergence.

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
section: The Components of RLHF Using PPO
text:
The Components of RLHF Using PPO
RLHF with PPO famously requires four copies of the network in memory at once. These models share identical architectures but their tasks are different.








model
role
trained?




policy
generates responses; the model we are improving
yes


reference
frozen SFT (instruction tuned) snapshot; anchors the KL penalty
no


reward model
the judge; scores finished responses
no


critic
predicts the expected future reward from each prefix
yes



The critic is initialized from the trained reward model, which already knows how to read response quality. However, now it needs to learn to predict it from partial responses.






Note



With GPT-2 medium this is roughly 1.4B parameters loaded in memory, before optimizer state. This is why RLHF has a reputation for being infrastructure-hungry.


We load the required networks and define the necessary hyperparameters.

policy_model = load_sft_model() # the model we will train
reference_model = nnx.clone(policy_model) # frozen SFT snapshot
critic_model = nnx.clone(reward_model)  # value function, initialized from the trained RM

PROMPTS_PER_ITERATION = 8 # fresh prompts sampled per PPO iteration
GROUP_SIZE = 4 # completions sampled per prompt
MAX_NEW_TOKENS = 35 # response length cap
NUM_ITERATIONS = 20 # 8 * 4 = 32 episodes per iteration, 640 episodes total

KL_COEF = 0.1 # beta: strength of the per-token KL constraint
MISSING_EOS_PENALTY = -1.0 # terminal reward for a response that never finished
CLIP_EPS = 0.2 # PPO clipping radius
VF_COEF = 0.1 # weight of the critic's loss
GAMMA = 1.0 # no discounting within a response
LAM = 0.95 # GAE lambda
PPO_EPOCHS = 2 # optimization passes over each rollout buffer
MINIBATCH_SIZE = 8 # sequences per gradient step
POLICY_LR = 1e-5
CRITIC_LR = 1e-5

# keeps every minibatch the same shape, so jit compiles the update exactly once
assert (PROMPTS_PER_ITERATION * GROUP_SIZE) % MINIBATCH_SIZE == 0

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Phase 1: Collecting Experience
PPO is (mostly) on-policy, which means that the experience it learns from must come from the current policy. Each iteration starts by sampling responses. Two details are easy to get wrong:

Sample at temperature 1 with no top-k or nucleus truncation. The math assumes the distribution we sampled from is the policy. Truncated sampling would make the recorded log-probabilities wrong, silently biasing every update.
Exploration comes from sampling itself. Greedy decoding would collect the same response every time and learn nothing new.

We sample GROUP_SIZE completions of the same prompt as one batch. This is a deliberate trick because a batch of identical prompts needs no padding during generation, so our padding-mask-free model can generate correctly.






Note



Production systems batch different prompts using left-padding, attention masks, and KV caches — machinery our small model doesn’t need.


After generation, every rollout is right-padded to one fixed length LMAX so that all downstream jitted computations compile exactly once.

train_prompts = [
    np.array(tokenizer.encode(format_input(entry) + "\n\n### Response:\n"))
    for entry in train_data
]

max_prompt_len = max(len(p) for p in train_prompts)
LMAX = max_prompt_len + MAX_NEW_TOKENS
assert LMAX + 1 <= config["context_length"]  # +1: the reward model gets a column for a trailing <|endoftext|>
print(f"Longest prompt: {max_prompt_len} tokens -> every rollout padded to {LMAX} tokens")


def sample_group(policy, prompt_ids, group_size, max_new_tokens, rng_key, temperature=1.0):
    """Sample `group_size` completions of the same prompt in one batch."""
    idx = jnp.tile(jnp.asarray(prompt_ids)[None, :], (group_size, 1))
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        logits = policy(idx)[:, -1, :] / temperature
        rng_key, subkey = jax.random.split(rng_key)
        next_token = jax.random.categorical(subkey, logits, axis=-1)
        idx = jnp.concatenate([idx, next_token[:, None]], axis=1)
    return idx

Longest prompt: 65 tokens -> every rollout padded to 100 tokens



Scoring a Rollout
For every sampled sequence, PPO needs four quantities:

\(\log \pi(a_t \mid s_t)\): the policy’s log-probability of each response token,
\(\log \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a_t \mid s_t)\): the same, under the frozen reference,
\(V(s_t)\): the critic’s value estimate at each prefix,
\(r_\phi(x, y)\): the reward model’s score for the finished response.

A convenient property of causal transformers is that we don’t need to record probabilities during the sampling loop. One forward pass over the finished sequence produces the logits at every position simultaneously, the output at position \(t\) is the distribution over token \(t{+}1\), so a single pass recovers every per-token log-probability. All four quantities come from one jitted function.
The response mask marks which of the \(T{-}1\) next-token positions are actions we are training. This includes the response tokens, up to and including the first <|endoftext|> (choosing to stop is an action too), and nothing after it. Positions outside the mask, such as the prompt, and padding, are excluded from every loss and every mean.
The reward model needs a different treatment, and we need to be careful here. During training we appended <|endoftext|> to every pair and read the score there, so that is the only kind of position the RM has ever learned to score. A sampled rollout that spends its entire MAX_NEW_TOKENS budget without emitting <|endoftext|> ends mid-sentence, and scoring it where it happens to stop asks the RM a question it was never trained to answer. So the RM reads one position further on those rollouts, landing on the trailing <|endoftext|>. Note that this is a different index from the last action, but the terminal reward still attaches to the final real response token, since a padding position is not something the policy chose.
That fixes the position the score is read at, but not the deeper problem that the text is still a fragment, and the RM cannot grade half a sentence or a mid-word token. So instead when a rollout never terminates we apply a fixed MISSING_EOS_PENALTY as its terminal reward.
It is worth being clear about why we penalize these rather than simply dropping them, which is the tempting alternative. PPO estimates an expectation over the policy’s own output distribution, and discarding the rollouts that ran long makes length a hidden selection criterion, and we would end up optimizing the policy conditioned on having stopped early. Moreover, the deleted rollouts are precisely the rambling ones, so never finishing would become the one behavior that escapes criticism entirely. Keeping the sample and scoring it badly is what teaches the policy to stop.

def token_logprobs(model, sequences):
    """Log-probability the model assigns to each next token: output[:, t] scores sequences[:, t+1]."""
    logits = model(sequences[:, :-1])
    logps = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits, axis=-1)
    return jnp.take_along_axis(logps, sequences[:, 1:, None], axis=-1).squeeze(-1)


def build_response_mask(sequences, prompt_len, eos_id=EOS_ID):
    """1.0 at response-token positions (in the T-1 next-token grid), up to and including the first <|endoftext|>.

    Must be called on the raw (unpadded) rollouts, so that padding cannot be mistaken for a generated end-of-text.
    """
    sequences = np.asarray(sequences)
    responses = sequences[:, prompt_len:]
    is_eos = (responses == eos_id).astype(np.int64)
    after_first_eos = np.cumsum(is_eos, axis=1) - is_eos # > 0 strictly after the first eos
    response_mask = (after_first_eos == 0).astype(np.float32)
    mask = np.zeros((sequences.shape[0], sequences.shape[1] - 1), dtype=np.float32)
    mask[:, prompt_len - 1:] = response_mask
    return mask


def pad_to_lmax(sequences, pad_id=PAD_ID):
    sequences = np.asarray(sequences)
    return np.pad(sequences, ((0, 0), (0, LMAX - sequences.shape[1])), constant_values=pad_id)


def rm_view(sequences, prompt_len, response_lengths, has_eos):
    """The reward model's own copy of the rollouts, always read at an <|endoftext|>.

    A rollout that doesn't emit one ends on an ordinary token, which the RM never learned to score.
    Reading one position further lands on the trailing <|endoftext|>. This ensures our RM doesn't
    score mid-sentence tokens.
    """
    last_token_idx = prompt_len - 1 + response_lengths
    rm_idx = np.where(has_eos, last_token_idx, last_token_idx + 1).astype(np.int32)
    rm_sequences = np.pad(sequences, ((0, 0), (0, 1)), constant_values=EOS_ID)
    return rm_sequences, rm_idx


@nnx.jit
def score_rollouts(policy, reference, reward_model, critic, sequences, rm_sequences, rm_idx):
    """Everything PPO needs to know about a batch of finished rollouts, in one jitted pass."""
    logprobs = token_logprobs(policy, sequences)        # (batch, LMAX-1)
    ref_logprobs = token_logprobs(reference, sequences) # (batch, LMAX-1)
    values = critic(sequences[:, :-1])                  # (batch, LMAX-1): V(s_t) at every prefix
    rm_scores = jnp.take_along_axis(reward_model(rm_sequences), rm_idx[:, None], axis=1).squeeze(-1)
    return logprobs, ref_logprobs, values, rm_scores



From Rewards to Advantages
A policy-gradient method increases the log-probability of each action in proportion to how good its outcome was. Using the raw return as “how good” is statistically terrible because almost every completion earns some reward, so every sampled token gets pushed up, just by different amounts resulting in a very noisy signal. What we actually want to know is whether an action made things better than expected.
“Expected” is exactly what the critic provides, \(V(s_t)\), an estimate of the reward that will eventually arrive if we continue from prefix \(s_t\). Subtracting it centers the learning signal, where the advantage \(\hat{A}_t > 0\) implies the action worked out better than the critic predicted, whereas advantages \(< 0\) are worse than expected. This is also why a terminal-only reward still teaches every token because the critic redistributes the end-of-episode signal across the response, and each token is credited with how much it changed the outlook.
We estimate advantages with Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) (Schulman et al. 2015). Define the one-step surprise (Temporal-Difference error):
\[\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\]
and accumulate it backwards over the episode with a decay \(\lambda\):
\[\hat{A}_t = \sum_{k \ge 0} (\gamma \lambda)^k \, \delta_{t+k}\]
\(\lambda\) interpolates between trusting the critic completely (\(\lambda{=}0\): low variance, biased by critic errors) and trusting only observed rewards (\(\lambda{=}1\): unbiased, high variance). We use the customary \(\lambda{=}0.95\), and discount factor of \(\gamma{=}1\) because a 35-token response is a short episode and there is no reason to value late reward less. The critic itself is trained toward the returns \(\hat{A}_t + V(s_t)\).
Finally we whiten/standardize advantages (zero mean, unit variance) across each rollout buffer. This is a standard variance-reduction trick that also makes the model robust to the RM’s arbitrary scale.

def masked_mean(x, mask, axis=None):
    return jnp.sum(x * mask, axis=axis) / jnp.maximum(jnp.sum(mask, axis=axis), 1e-8)


def masked_whiten(x, mask):
    mean = masked_mean(x, mask)
    var = masked_mean((x - mean) ** 2, mask)
    return (x - mean) * jax.lax.rsqrt(var + 1e-8) * mask


def compute_gae(rewards, values, mask, gamma=GAMMA, lam=LAM):
    """Generalized Advantage Estimation"""
    batch, horizon = rewards.shape
    advantages = np.zeros_like(rewards)
    last_gae = np.zeros(batch)
    for t in reversed(range(horizon)):
        next_values = values[:, t + 1] if t < horizon - 1 else 0.0
        next_mask = mask[:, t + 1] if t < horizon - 1 else 0.0   # 0 past the episode boundary
        delta = rewards[:, t] + gamma * next_values * next_mask - values[:, t]
        last_gae = delta + gamma * lam * next_mask * last_gae
        advantages[:, t] = last_gae
    advantages = advantages * mask
    returns = advantages + values * mask
    return advantages, returns

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Phase 2: The PPO Objective
Rollouts are expensive, so we want several gradient steps per batch of experience. But after the first step the policy no longer matches the policy that generated the data. PPO applies two fixes to get around this issue.
First, an importance ratio per token corrects for the mismatch:
\[\rho_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}\]
Second, the ratio is clipped, so the objective stops rewarding movement beyond a trust region of the sampling policy:
\[\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_t\Big[ \min\big( \rho_t \hat{A}_t,\;\; \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t,\, 1{-}\epsilon,\, 1{+}\epsilon)\, \hat{A}_t \big) \Big]\]
As long as \(\rho_t\) stays inside \([1{-}\epsilon,\, 1{+}\epsilon]\) this is the ordinary policy gradient. Once the policy has already moved a token’s probability by more than \(\epsilon\) in the direction its advantage points, the min selects the clipped branch, the objective goes flat, and that token contributes zero gradient. Stale data can never push the policy too far.
On our very first minibatch \(\pi_\theta = \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}\), so every \(\rho_t = 1\) (this is why dropout had to go). The clip fraction which represents the share of tokens whose ratio has left the trust region is a good metric to monitor because near 0 means we are barely using the trust region, while a large fraction means the policy is moving fast and the clip is preventing large policy changes.
The critic is trained alongside the policy with a mean-squared error toward the returns, and both models get global-norm gradient clipping which is standard PPO hygiene.

def ppo_loss_fn(policy, critic, sequences, mask, old_logprobs, advantages, returns):
    logprobs = token_logprobs(policy, sequences)
    ratio = jnp.exp(logprobs - old_logprobs)

    pg_loss_unclipped = -advantages * ratio
    pg_loss_clipped = -advantages * jnp.clip(ratio, 1.0 - CLIP_EPS, 1.0 + CLIP_EPS)
    pg_loss = masked_mean(jnp.maximum(pg_loss_unclipped, pg_loss_clipped), mask)

    values = critic(sequences[:, :-1])
    vf_loss = 0.5 * masked_mean((values - returns) ** 2, mask)

    loss = pg_loss + VF_COEF * vf_loss
    clip_fraction = masked_mean((jnp.abs(ratio - 1.0) > CLIP_EPS).astype(jnp.float32), mask)
    return loss, {"pg_loss": pg_loss, "vf_loss": vf_loss, "clip_fraction": clip_fraction}


policy_optimizer = nnx.Optimizer(
    policy_model,
    optax.chain(optax.clip_by_global_norm(1.0), optax.adamw(POLICY_LR, weight_decay=0.0)),
    wrt=nnx.Param,
)
critic_optimizer = nnx.Optimizer(
    critic_model,
    optax.chain(optax.clip_by_global_norm(1.0), optax.adamw(CRITIC_LR, weight_decay=0.0)),
    wrt=nnx.Param,
)


@nnx.jit
def ppo_train_step(
    policy,
    critic,
    policy_optimizer,
    critic_optimizer,
    sequences,
    mask,
    old_logprobs,
    advantages,
    returns
):
    grad_fn = nnx.value_and_grad(ppo_loss_fn, argnums=(0, 1), has_aux=True)
    (loss, stats), (policy_grads, critic_grads) = grad_fn(
        policy, critic, sequences, mask, old_logprobs, advantages, returns
    )
    policy_optimizer.update(policy, policy_grads)
    critic_optimizer.update(critic, critic_grads)
    return loss, stats

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
The RLHF Training Loop
Each iteration has the two phases we built above:

Phase 1 (collect). With parameters frozen, sample a group of completions for each of PROMPTS_PER_ITERATION prompts then score everything (log-probs, reference log-probs, values, RM scores) and assemble per-token rewards + run GAE.
Phase 2 (optimize). Make PPO_EPOCHS shuffled minibatch passes over the buffer with the clipped objective.

What to watch while it runs:

The reward: the mean RM score of fresh samples. This is the number RLHF exists to increase.
KL/token: the drift from the SFT model. It should grow slowly; if it explodes, the constraint (\(\beta\)) is too loose or the learning rate is too high.
unfinished: the share of rollouts that hit the token cap without emitting <|endoftext|>, and therefore collected MISSING_EOS_PENALTY instead of a real score. It should fall as training proceeds. If it stays high, the reward signal is mostly this penalty rather than anything about politeness, and either the cap or the penalty needs revisiting.
clip fraction: It is exactly 0 on the first minibatch of each iteration and grows across the PPO_EPOCHS passes. A per-iteration average that settles above ~0.3 is a sign the policy is moving too far per batch, and calls for a lower learning rate or fewer epochs.







Warning



A practical note on runtime: sampling token-by-token without a KV cache dominates the cost, so expect a few minutes per iteration on CPU.



sample_rng = jax.random.PRNGKey(42)
shuffle_rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
prompt_queue = []

reward_history = []
kl_history = []
length_history = []
clip_history = []
unfinished_history = []

for iteration in range(NUM_ITERATIONS):
    # Phase 1: collect experience with the current policy (our trained language model)
    buffer = {"sequences": [], "masks": [], "logprobs": [], "advantages": [], "returns": []}
    iter_scores, iter_kls, iter_lengths, iter_unfinished = [], [], [], []
    sample_completion = None

    for _ in tqdm(range(PROMPTS_PER_ITERATION), desc=f"iter {iteration}: rollouts", leave=False):
        if not prompt_queue:
            prompt_queue = list(shuffle_rng.permutation(len(train_prompts)))
        prompt_ids = train_prompts[prompt_queue.pop()]
        prompt_len = len(prompt_ids)

        sample_rng, sample_key = jax.random.split(sample_rng)
        rollouts = sample_group(policy_model, prompt_ids, GROUP_SIZE, MAX_NEW_TOKENS, sample_key)

        mask = build_response_mask(rollouts, prompt_len)   # before padding: pads must not look like actions
        sequences = pad_to_lmax(rollouts)
        full_mask = np.zeros((GROUP_SIZE, LMAX - 1), dtype=np.float32)
        full_mask[:, :mask.shape[1]] = mask

        response_lengths = full_mask.sum(axis=1)
        last_token_idx = (prompt_len - 1 + response_lengths).astype(np.int32)  # last response token of each rollout
        has_eos = (np.asarray(rollouts)[:, prompt_len:] == EOS_ID).any(axis=1)
        rm_sequences, rm_idx = rm_view(sequences, prompt_len, response_lengths, has_eos)

        logprobs, ref_logprobs, values, rm_scores = score_rollouts(
            policy_model, reference_model, reward_model, critic_model,
            jnp.asarray(sequences), jnp.asarray(rm_sequences), jnp.asarray(rm_idx),
        )
        logprobs, ref_logprobs, values, rm_scores = map(
            np.asarray, (logprobs, ref_logprobs, values, rm_scores)
        )
        # Penalize a response that didn't emit an end token
        rm_scores = np.where(has_eos, rm_scores, MISSING_EOS_PENALTY)

        kl = (logprobs - ref_logprobs) * full_mask
        rewards = -KL_COEF * kl
        rewards[np.arange(GROUP_SIZE), last_token_idx - 1] += rm_scores  # the RM applied at the EOS position

        advantages, returns = compute_gae(rewards, values, full_mask)

        buffer["sequences"].append(sequences)
        buffer["masks"].append(full_mask)
        buffer["logprobs"].append(logprobs)
        buffer["advantages"].append(advantages)
        buffer["returns"].append(returns)

        iter_scores.append(rm_scores.mean())
        iter_kls.append(kl.sum() / full_mask.sum())
        iter_lengths.append(response_lengths.mean())
        iter_unfinished.append(1.0 - has_eos.mean())
        if sample_completion is None:
            sample_completion = tokenizer.decode(sequences[0, prompt_len:last_token_idx[0] + 1].tolist())

    # Phase 2: several PPO passes over the buffer
    sequences = jnp.asarray(np.concatenate(buffer["sequences"]))
    masks = jnp.asarray(np.concatenate(buffer["masks"]))
    old_logprobs = jnp.asarray(np.concatenate(buffer["logprobs"]))
    returns = jnp.asarray(np.concatenate(buffer["returns"]))
    advantages = masked_whiten(jnp.asarray(np.concatenate(buffer["advantages"])), masks)

    num_sequences = sequences.shape[0]
    iter_clip_fractions = []
    for _ in range(PPO_EPOCHS):
        permutation = shuffle_rng.permutation(num_sequences)
        for start in range(0, num_sequences, MINIBATCH_SIZE):
            minibatch = permutation[start:start + MINIBATCH_SIZE]
            loss, stats = ppo_train_step(
                policy_model, critic_model, policy_optimizer, critic_optimizer,
                sequences[minibatch], masks[minibatch], old_logprobs[minibatch],
                advantages[minibatch], returns[minibatch],
            )
            iter_clip_fractions.append(float(stats["clip_fraction"]))

    reward_history.append(float(np.mean(iter_scores)))
    kl_history.append(float(np.mean(iter_kls)))
    length_history.append(float(np.mean(iter_lengths)))
    clip_history.append(float(np.mean(iter_clip_fractions)))
    unfinished_history.append(float(np.mean(iter_unfinished)))

    print(
        f"iter {iteration:>3} | reward {reward_history[-1]:+.3f} | KL/token {kl_history[-1]:+.4f} "
        f"| resp len {length_history[-1]:4.1f} | unfinished {unfinished_history[-1]:.0%} "
        f"| clip frac {clip_history[-1]:.2f}"
    )
    if iteration % 5 == 0:
        print(f"          sample: {sample_completion!r}")

title: Building a Large Language ModelPart 3: GPT RLHF
text:
Alternative Approaches to PPO
Classic RLHF is no longer the only game in town, and knowing it makes the alternatives easy to read:

Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al. 2023) collapses the reward model and the RL loop into a single supervised loss applied directly to preference pairs — a closed-form shortcut through everything we built in this post. No rollouts, no critic, one model plus a frozen reference.
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al. 2024) keeps the RL loop but drops the critic. Sample a group of responses per prompt and use each sample’s z-score within its group as the advantage. Our rollout code already samples in groups. Try replacing GAE with a group baseline as an exercise.
REINFORCE Leave-One-Out (RLOO) and related REINFORCE variants (Ahmadian et al. 2024) make a similar critic-free trade as GRPO, with a leave-one-out baseline instead of the group baseline.
Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) replaces the learned reward model with verifiable rewards such as unit tests and math checkers, and powers the current generation of reasoning models (Lambert et al. 2024).

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBonus: Text-Classification
text: We expand on the hands-on example of the last post and show how we can leverage TF-IDF sparse embeddings to build a multinomial logistic regression classifier.

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBonus: Text-Classification
text:
Vanilla MLR:
\[
y \sim Categorical(\textbf{p})
\]
\[
\textbf{p} = softmax(\pmb{\alpha} + \pmb{\beta}\textbf{X})
\]
\[
\pmb{\alpha} \sim Normal(0, 1)
\]
\[
\pmb{\beta} \sim Normal(0, 0.5)
\]
Also remember that we are constraining our model such that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_{k} = 0
\]
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\beta_{kd} = 0
\]
Where we have \(k\) classes and \(d\) features.






Caution



We discussed the two different ways to impose identifiability to our model and talked about the nice property of having all the coefficients available to us using the sum to zero constraint. It is important to mention that the drawback is that this method is slower because you are explicitly estimating those coefficients.

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBonus: Text-Classification
text:
Structured Covariance MLR
In order to address IIA we need to model the correlations between class-wise coefficients. We can model it like
\[
y \sim Categorical(\textbf{p})
\]
\[
\textbf{p} = softmax(\pmb{\alpha} + \pmb{\beta}\textbf{X})
\]
\[
\pmb{\alpha} \sim Normal(0, 1)
\]
\[
\pmb{\beta} \sim MVNormal(\textbf{0}, \pmb{\Sigma}_{class})
\]
\[
\pmb{\Sigma}_{class} \sim \textbf{LKJ}(2.0)
\]
In this model we specifically model the covariance between the coefficients across classes by placing an \(LKJ(\eta)\) prior on the covariance matrix. The \(\eta\) parameter adjusts our prior belief on how strong/weak we expect the coefficients to be correlated.
Where

\(\eta = 1\) places a uniform distribution over the correlation matrices
\(\eta \lt 1\) places more weight over the coefficients being correlated and
\(\eta \gt 1\) places lesser weight over the coefficients being correlated

In our example we set \(\eta = 2.0\) because our prior belief is that in this particular example the correlations between class coefficients will be small.

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBonus: Text-Classification
text:
Setup
Let’s go ahead and pull the code from the prior post that pulls in the toy dataset and generates the TF-IDF embeddings.

# imports
import re
from collections import Counter
from typing import Literal

import arviz as az
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import pymc as pm
import pytensor.sparse as spt
import pytensor.tensor as pt
import xarray as xr
from numpy.typing import NDArray
from scipy import stats
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_20newsgroups
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix


# Set a seed for reproducibility
seed = sum(map(ord, "multinomialLR"))
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)


# TF-IDF Functions
def tokenize(text: str, TOKEN_PATTERN = re.compile(r"(?u)\b\w\w+\b")) -> list[str]:
    tokens = TOKEN_PATTERN.findall(text.lower())
    return tokens

def tf_log(count):
    return 1 + np.log10(count)

def idf(doc_count, num_documents):
    return np.log10(num_documents / doc_count)

def tf_idf(vocabulary: list, tokens: list[list], mode: Literal['fit', 'transform'] = "fit") -> NDArray:
    """
    Creates sparse TF-IDF embeddings from a given vocabulary and the tokens of documents

    Parameters
    ----------
    vocabulary: list
        The total unique words in your training set corpus
    tokens: list[list]
        a list of documents' list of tokens
    mode: Literal
        whether you are fitting on a new corpus or transforming to an already existing corpus. default (fit)

    Returns
    -------
    NDArray
        The sparse embeddings in a dense representation
    """

    doc_term_counts = [Counter(doc) for doc in tokens]

    # Compute TF matrix: rows = terms, columns = documents
    term_frequencies = []
    for term in vocabulary:
        term_frequencies.append([
            tf_log(doc.get(term, 0)) if doc.get(term, 0) > 0 else 0
            for doc in doc_term_counts
        ])
    term_frequencies = np.array(term_frequencies)

    num_documents = term_frequencies.shape[1]

    document_frequencies = np.sum(term_frequencies > 0, axis=1)

    if mode == "fit":
        inverse_document_frequencies = []
        for doc_count in document_frequencies:
            inverse_document_frequencies.append(idf(doc_count, num_documents))

        inverse_document_frequencies = np.array(inverse_document_frequencies)
    else:
        inverse_document_frequencies = []
        for doc_count in document_frequencies:
            if doc_count > 0:
                inverse_document_frequencies.append(idf(doc_count, num_documents))
            else:
                inverse_document_frequencies.append(0)
        inverse_document_frequencies = np.array(inverse_document_frequencies)

    return term_frequencies * inverse_document_frequencies[:, None]


# Pull in toy data
categories = [
    "sci.med",
    "comp.graphics",
    "sci.space",
]

newsgroups_train = fetch_20newsgroups(subset='train', categories=categories)
newsgroups_test = fetch_20newsgroups(subset='test', categories=categories)


# Create training dataset TF-IDF
train_tokens = [tokenize(text) for text in newsgroups_train.data]
vocabulary = sorted(set(sum(train_tokens, [])))
train_tf_idf = tf_idf(vocabulary=vocabulary, tokens=train_tokens, mode='fit')

# Create testing dataset TF-IDF
test_tokens = [tokenize(text) for text in newsgroups_test.data]
test_tf_idf = tf_idf(vocabulary=vocabulary, tokens=test_tokens, mode='transform')

# Create X,y sets
X_train = train_tf_idf.T
y_train = newsgroups_train.target
X_test = test_tf_idf.T
y_test = newsgroups_test.target

Here we will convert our sparse matrices from the dense representation with all the zeros to the CSR representation that we discussed above.

# Create Sparse CSR Matrices
X_train_sparse = csr_matrix(X_train)
X_test_sparse = csr_matrix(X_test)

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBonus: Text-Classification
text:
Vanilla MLR
Alright, with our TF-IDF embeddings created and converted to CSR we are ready to start building our model. Let’s start with the typical “vanilla” MLR model that assumes IIA. We are going to be doing all of this in a Bayesian framework which gives us the flexibility to extend this “vanilla” model to include more complex relationships.
Notice that we are enforcing identifiability by inducing a sum to zero over the parameters across the classes and notice that we are computing our logits using a sparse matrix vector multiplication algorithm.

# MLR Model specification
coords = {
    "classes": newsgroups_test.target_names,
    "features": vocabulary,
    "num_obs": np.arange(X_train.shape[0])
}
with pm.Model(coords=coords) as sparse_model:
    # Data containers
    y = pm.Data("y", y_train, dims="num_obs")
    X = pm.Data("X", X_train_sparse)

    # Priors
    # Unconstrained raw parameters
    alpha_raw = pm.Normal("alpha_raw", 0, 1, dims="classes")
    coefs_raw = pm.Normal("coefs_raw", 0, 0.5, dims=("classes", "features"))

    # Enforce identifiability by subtracting mean across the class dimension
    alpha = alpha_raw - pt.mean(alpha_raw)
    coefs = coefs_raw - pt.mean(coefs_raw, axis=0)

    # Compute logits using sparse dot
    logits = alpha + spt.structured_dot(X, coefs.T)

    # Likelihood
    pm.Categorical("y_obs", logit_p=logits, observed=y, dims="num_obs")

One thing to note is that at the moment sparse tensor operations are not supported in sampling accelerators like nutpie or numpyro via PyMC. So we will have to sample with the default PyMC sampler.

# Sampling
with sparse_model:
    idata = pm.sample(mp_ctx="spawn", random_seed=rng)

With our samples in hand, let’s pull a summary of the learned weights and inspect what words based on the TF-IDF embeddings have the largest influence over each class.

title: How Machines Comprehend LanguageBonus: Text-Classification
text:
Structured Covariance MLR
Let’s extend the previous model to handle IIA.
As mentioned above, we are setting our prior to assume that the correlations between the classes are minute. However, with the large volume of data used for sampling, if this prior is not appropriate the likelihood will adjust our covariance weights to reflect that.
Notice here, we are working with our coefficients in the transposed space which changes the axis used to induce our sum to zero constraint.






Warning



This model is more complex and as such requires more samples. Below we increased the number of chains to acquire more samples while leveraging parallel computing. If your machine has less than 8 cores, you will need to adjust the number of chains accordingly.



# Features and classes
D = X_train_sparse.shape[1]
K = 3

with pm.Model(coords=coords) as sparse_correlated_model:
    # Data containers
    y = pm.Data("y", y_train, dims="num_obs")
    X = pm.Data("X", X_train_sparse)

    # Priors
    # Unconstrained raw parameters
    alpha_raw = pm.Normal("alpha_raw", 0, 1, dims="classes")

    # Enforce identifiability by subtracting mean across the class dimension
    alpha = alpha_raw - pt.mean(alpha_raw)

    # covariance prior
    sd_dist = pm.HalfNormal.dist(1.0)
    chol, corr, stds = pm.LKJCholeskyCov(
        "class_cov", n=K, eta=2.0, sd_dist=sd_dist
    )

    # non-centered parameterization for better sampling
    z = pm.Normal("z", mu=0, sigma=1, shape=(D, K), dims=("features", "classes"))
    coefs_T = pm.Deterministic("coefs_T", pt.dot(z, chol.T), dims=("features", "classes"))

    # Enforce identifiability by subtracting mean across the class dimension
    coefs_T_constrained = coefs_T - pt.mean(coefs_T, axis=1, keepdims=True)

    # Compute logits using sparse dot
    logits = alpha + spt.structured_dot(X, coefs_T_constrained)

    # Likelihood
    pm.Categorical("y_obs", logit_p=logits, observed=y, dims="num_obs")

with sparse_correlated_model:
    correlated_idata = pm.sample(mp_ctx="spawn", target_accept=0.9, cores=8, random_seed=rng)
